display.title: Mesiras Nefesh of a Child, Part 1
display.summary_short: For Yud-Beis Tammuz: as an eleven-year-old in Lubavitch, the Frierdiker Rebbe stands up for a poor butcher struck by a policeman and is locked in a dark jail cell.
display.summary_long: On Yud-Beis Tammuz, the Frierdiker Rebbe's festival of liberation, the storyteller explains the opening of the discourse the Rebbe asked us to learn that day: when even one Jew sits and learns Torah, the Shechinah rests there. He explains that mesiras nefesh also means giving over our own will to Hashem. Then, in the Frierdiker Rebbe's own words, the story: at eleven he had earned thirty rubles for knowing two orders of Mishnayos by heart and used them for a free-loan fund, keeping careful books. One borrower was Reb Dovid the butcher, a poor, simple, cheerful Jew who never missed the sunrise minyan. One summer market day in 1891, while his parents were away, the boy saw a policeman strike Reb Dovid so hard his nose bled. He shouted and pushed the policeman, and was dragged to the police station, slapped and locked in a dark room. Frightened by strange noises, he reviewed Mishnayos by heart and davened Mincha with joy, feeling it was a Yom Tov to suffer for helping a Jew. What happens next? To be continued.
display.lesson: Stand up for a fellow Jew even at a cost, and keep Torah in your head so you can learn wherever you are.

The boy is locked alone in a dark jail room for a few hours.
